name: 四季彩菜 一条 東向通店 (Shikisaisai Ichijo Higashimukidori-ten)

claims.text: Menu is built on sashimi, fried/battered items (cartilage karaage, potato-mochi cheese fritters), soy-sauce and ponzu dressings — high gluten exposure with no GF protocol documented.
Standard izakaya soy sauce and ponzu (wheat-containing) are used throughout for sashimi and dishes; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Vegetable dishes and salads are typical izakaya fare likely seasoned with fish dashi or bonito; no vegan preparation is documented and seafood dominates the kitchen.

name: そば処 喜多原 (Soba-dokoro Kitahara)

claims.text: The soba itself is 90% buckwheat / 10% wheat (gai-ichi), so the noodles contain wheat; tempura batter and a shared kitchen mean wheat is present throughout. Not suitable for gluten avoidance.
Traditional soba tsuyu is soy-sauce based, which normally contains wheat; no wheat-free broth is documented.
Soba broth (tsuyu/soba-yu) at a classic soba shop is made with fish-based dashi, and tempura share fryer/kitchen with seafood items, so cross-contact with animal products is likely.
Buckwheat is stone-milled in-house each morning and the soba is hand-cut and boiled to order, so ingredients are fresh and the menu is simple and transparent.
Soba noodles are made with an 8:2 wheat-to-buckwheat blend, so they are not gluten-free; tempura is wheat-battered and prepared in the same small kitchen.
Soba is served with a traditional dashi-and-soy broth, which is typically wheat-containing soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.
The broth is fish-based dashi and the kitchen centers on eel and tempura, so vegan cross-contact is likely; no separate vegan preparation is documented.
Wheat-batter tempura and kakiage are fried in the same small kitchen as the soba, with no documented separation, so cross-contact with wheat is likely.
The soba is served with a soy-sauce-based dashi (bonito, horse mackerel, Rausu kombu); standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and no gluten-free alternative is documented.
The dashi/broth is fish-based (bonito and horse mackerel), so even the noodle dishes are not vegan.

name: そば切り 百夜月 (Sobakiri Momoyozuki)

claims.text: A soba kitchen serving both nihachi (wheat-blended) and jūwari noodles cooked in shared water means heavy wheat cross-contact; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
The dipping broth/tsuyu uses standard soy sauce, which normally contains wheat.
Broths are based on fish dashi, and seasonal dishes include duck-broth soba, so dishes are not vegan.
No published gluten-free/allergen policy and no reservations; celiac accommodations must be requested in person and are unverified.
Genuine jūwari (100% buckwheat) and a hand-ground tebiki soba (10/day) are on the menu, so a wheat-free noodle is actually available.
Stone-ground flour and hand-cut noodles; rare Hiroshima Hiba heirloom buckwheat for the tebiki.

name: 蕎麦切り 西本 (Sobakiri Nishimoto)

claims.text: Soba is a 二八 (2:8) blend containing wheat flour, and tempura is wheat-battered and fried, so wheat is pervasive in the kitchen.
Standard soba tsuyu and warm soup are made with wheat-containing Japanese soy sauce; no wheat-free tamari is documented.
Dipping broth and soups are fish-dashi based and some sets include egg and grated yam; duck dishes use animal stock.
This is a working sourdough bakery; wheat and rye flour are central to the entire operation, so airborne flour and shared surfaces make cross-contamination effectively unavoidable for celiac diners.
Breads and sandwiches share the same kitchen and counter as dairy and meat fillings; no separate vegan preparation is documented.
The owner speaks fluent English, so allergy or ingredient questions can be discussed directly, though no formal allergen handling is documented.
Bread is made in-house from wild-yeast and lactic-acid natural fermentation with carefully selected ingredients, and the English-speaking owner can answer ingredient questions.

name: すするか、すすらんか。 (Susuruka, Susuranka.)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles are the foundation of every bowl and are boiled in shared water; the mapo sauce uses doubanjiang and fermented-soybean pastes that typically contain wheat. No gluten-free preparation is documented.
The mapo tofu base relies on doubanjiang and fermented soybeans, which are conventional wheat-containing fermented seasonings; no wheat-free seasoning is indicated.
Bowls are built on a chicken-bone broth with minced meat, so all preparation surfaces and broth contact animal products; no vegan option is documented.
